column2: Of this one made one, lord, the whole earth is not able to bear the energy; let him be created in many forms.
Thus addressed by Brahma, and his share too being assigned, the god said "So be it" to the blessed Brahma of immeasurable splendour.
The bearer of the Pinaka reached supreme joy, smiling, and Bhava then received his share as told by Brahma.
And the knower of all dharma then distributed the Fever in many ways for the peace of all beings; hear that also, dear.
Headache for the serpents; the shilajatu for mountains; know the blue colour for waters and the slough for snakes.
The khoraka disease for cows, saline soil on the earth, and for animals, knower of dharma, the blocking of sight.
For horses, a hollow in the body; for peacocks, the bursting of the crest; for cuckoos, eye disease: the great-souled one named the fever.
For lotuses, the splitting of the stamens; so we have heard; for all parrots, hiccup is called the fever.
For tigers, knower of dharma, fatigue is called the fever; among men, knower of dharma, it is known as fever by name, and enters a man at death, at birth and in between.
This is the energy of Maheshvara, Fever by name, so dreadful; the lord is to be bowed to and honoured by all creatures.
Entered by it, Vritra, best of upholders of dharma, yawned; then Shakra hurled the thunderbolt at him.
Entering Vritra, the thunderbolt split him, Bharata; and split by the thunderbolt, the great yogi, the great asura, went to the supreme seat of Vishnu of immeasurable splendour.
By devotion to Vishnu this world was pervaded by him formerly, and so, slain in battle, he reached Vishnu's abode.
Thus the extent of the great Fever, concerning Vritra, has been told by me, son; what else shall I tell you?
The man who with undismayed mind, collected, ever reads this origin of Fever is freed from disease, happy and glad, and gains the desires he wishes."
[Bhishma said:] "Here too they cite this ancient tale, the dialogue of Narada and Samanga, Bharata.
[Narada said:] 'You bow as it were with the chest, with the arms and with force; ever glad of mind, you seem free of grief.
I see no agitation in you here, even the subtlest; you act like a child, ever satisfied and at ease.'
[Samanga said:] 'The past, future and present in all beings, giver of honour: I know their truths, therefore I am not despondent.
I know the beginnings and again the rise of fruits; the fruits are varied in the world; therefore I am not despondent.
The unfathomable, the unfounded, the moving, Narada, the blind and the dull live; see us also living.
The dwellers of heaven, healthy of limb, live by what is ordained, strong and weak; honour us likewise.
Some live with thousands, some with hundreds, and others live on greens; see us also living.
The pride of a fool is delusion again; for the fool there is neither this world nor the other; sorrows do not come always, nor does happiness come always.
One like me would never feel fever over a state of turning being; he would not follow wished enjoyments or happiness, nor think of sorrow come.
Collected, he should not covet what is others'; he should not welcome gain that has come in various ways; nor rejoice at great gain of wealth, nor despair at its loss.
Neither kinsmen, nor wealth, nor family, nor learning, nor mantras, nor valour are able to save from sorrow; they do not go to peace hereafter except by character.
There is no intellect for the unjoined, no happiness without yoga; steadiness and giving up of sorrow, both bring happiness for us.
The dear brings joy, joy increases elation, and elation leads to hell alone; therefore I give it up.
These elations of grief and fear, bewilderers of pleasure and pain, I see like a witness in the world from the working of this body.
Giving up wealth and desire, free of grief and fever, giving up craving and delusion, I roam this earth.
I have no fear from death, adharma, greed, or from anything, as if I had drunk nectar, here or hereafter.
This I know, brahmana, having performed great imperishable austerity; therefore, Narada, grief does not trouble me.'"
[Bhishma said:] "Honouring the teacher always, attending the aged, and hearing the sciences: this is called the firm good.
Here too they cite this ancient tale, the dialogue of Galava and the divine sage Narada.
Galava said to Narada, a brahmana free of delusion and weariness, satisfied with knowledge, master of senses, wishing the good, self-controlled:
'By whatever qualities a man among men is esteemed in the world, I see all those qualities in you without fail.
You, being such, can cut our doubt, unbewildered among those long bewildered, not knowing the truth of the world.
For knowledge to make activity, one must know what should and should not be done; tell us what we do not determine to do.
Blessed one, all the stages of life, seeing separate conduct, run in different ways, saying "this is the good, this is the good."
Seeing them set out differently, each delighting in its shastras and content with its own shastras, we do not find the good.'
[Narada said:] 'Turning away from sinful action, constant merit-minded conduct, and good behaviour with the good: this is the good, without doubt.
Gentleness toward all beings, honesty in dealings, and sweet speech: this is the good, without doubt.
Sharing with gods and ancestors, and with guests, and not abandoning servants: this is the good, without doubt.
Speaking truth is good; knowing truth is hard; what is utterly for the good of beings, that I call truth.
Giving up ego, restraint of attachment, contentment and solitary living are called the firm good.
Study of the Veda by dharma, of the limbs of the Veda, and the inquiry into the aims of learning: this is the good, without doubt.
One wishing the good, scourge of foes, should not overindulge in sound, form, taste, touch and smell alone.
Night-roaming, sleeping by day, sloth, backbiting, pride, excess and neglect: one wishing the good should give these up.
One should not seek eminence of action by blaming others; one should seek distinction from the common man by one's own virtues.
Mostly it is the virtueless who think highly of themselves; they cast others with virtues down by faults, to diminish their own virtues.
And unspoken to again, puffed up with their own conceit, they think themselves better than great men.
Saying no blame of anyone and not describing his own worship, the wise man endowed with virtue gains great fame.
Without speaking, the pure fragrance of flowers blows; so without sounding, the spotless sun shines in the sky.
These and other things given up by the wise blaze with fame in the world, though they do not speak.
A fool does not shine in the world by praise of himself; the learned shines even when hidden in a pit.
A bad sound, though uttered loudly, dies down; but good speech shines slowly in the worlds.
The much talk of the foolish and the puffed up is empty; it shows the inner self as the sun shows form by day.
For this reason they seek wisdom of various kinds; gain of wisdom seems to me the best gain for beings.
One should speak to no one unasked, nor to one who asks improperly; though learned and wise, he should behave in the world like a dullard.
Then one should examine a dwelling among the good, ever constant in dharma, among generous men devoted to their own dharma.
One wishing the good should in no way live where mixing of dharma among the four classes occurs.
Here, even one who undertakes nothing, living on what comes, would gain merit among the meritorious and sin among the sinful, spotless.
As one feels the touch of water, fire and moon, so we find the touch of sin and merit in both.
Those eating the remains, not seeing the object of food, enjoy it; know the object of enjoyed food as the object of actions.
Where those who come are asked with disrespect and one would say the dharma of a brahmana, the self-possessed should leave that country.
Where the livelihood of teacher and disciple is well collected and endowed with scripture, who would leave that country?
Where those standing in the sky would surely speak a fault of the wise out of desire for self-worship, what sage would live there?
Where the bridges of dharma are mostly broken by the greedy, like the edge of a blazing mountain, who would not leave that country?
Where people practise dharma without fear, free of envy, there one should go and live among the good of holy character.
Where people practise dharma for the sake of wealth, one should never live with them, for they are doers of sin.
Where people live by sinful action, wishing to live, one should quickly run away, as from a snake, from the refuge.
The deed by which one climbs a cot and then repents should not be done at all by one wishing his own prosperity.
The self-possessed should leave the kingdom where the king and the king's men next in line are first eaters of the householders' food.
One should dwell in the kingdom where learned brahmanas are first to eat, eternal in dharma, devoted to officiating and teaching.
Where svaha, svadha and vashat are rightly performed and go on unceasingly, one should live there without deliberation.
Where one sees impure brahmanas worn by livelihood, he should leave that kingdom, as a bait that has been touched.
Where people give unasked, pleased, one should live with settled mind, as one self-possessed whose work is done.
Where punishment is for the undisciplined and honour for the self-trained, there one should go and live among the good of holy character.
For the afflicted, the unrestrained, the ill-conducted, the wicked, the undisciplined and the greedy, the great rod is kept.
Where the king is constant in dharma and attends to the kingdom, giving up desires, the lord of desires, one should live there without deliberation.
For kings of such character quickly join all dwellers of the land to the good when the good is at hand.
This good was told by me to you as you asked, dear; for the good of the self cannot be counted by the chief.
For one so acting, with a concentrated self, the good will become plain through austerity alone.'"
[Bhishma said:] "Here I shall relate to you an ancient tale told by Arishtanemi to Sagara, who asked.
[Sagara said:] 'Brahmana, what is the highest good, having done which one enjoys happiness here? How does one not grieve or be agitated? I wish to know this.'
[Bhishma said:] Thus addressed, Tarkshya, versed in all shastras, having understood the supreme wealth, spoke this good word.
'Happiness of liberation is happiness in the world, but the world does not understand it, attached to sons and cattle, filled with wealth and grain.
With attached mind and restless self he cannot be cured; bound by the snare of affection, the fool is not fit for liberation.
I shall tell you the snares born of affection; hear them; they can be cut by one who knows, with an attentive head.
When you have seen your sons grown in time to youth, married and capable of livelihood, know it and wander free as you please.
Know your wife, who has borne sons, who is aged, cherished and affectionate to the sons, and, considering the next world, leave her in time.
The freed, fearless, roam happily in the world; the attached perish; men there perish, without doubt.
Ants and worms that store food are unattached, happy in the world; the attached are the ones who perish.
With one seeking liberation, no concern should be had for his people: "How will these be without me?"
A creature is born of itself, grows of itself, and comes to pleasure, pain and death of itself.
In food and clothing, in the care of mother and father, they get by their own making; nothing was not made before.
All beings run about on the earth in the world with food ordained by the Creator, guarded by their own deeds.
For one who is himself a lump of clay and ever dependent, what reason is there to nourish or protect his people with an undeveloped self?
When death kills your own people before your eyes, even though great effort was made, you should understand it by yourself.
Even while he lives, you will leave him unfinished in his support and protection, and afterward you will die too.
When you are dead you will in no way know whether your people are happy or sad; should it not be understood by yourself?
Whether you are dead or alive, if people are to enjoy what they have made, knowing this one should do what is good for oneself.
Knowing this in this world, having settled "who is whose," set your mind on liberation and ponder it again.
One in whom hunger, thirst and the rest, anger, greed and delusion have been conquered, the one endowed with goodness, is indeed freed.
The man who is never heedless through bewilderment in dice, drink, women and hunting is indeed freed.
He who is tired of "food must be eaten day after day and night after night" is said to have a mind of faults.
He who ever sees, joined, the nature of the self in women, as freed again and again, rightly, is indeed freed.
He who truly knows the origin and destruction of beings and their doings in this world is indeed freed.
He who sees travel on thousands of vehicles and for crores of reasons, and the standing on a couch in a palace, is freed.
He who sees the world struck by death, afflicted by disease, and wasted for lack of livelihood is freed.
He who sees, happy and content, and who, not seeing, is not struck, and who is content with little in this world, is indeed freed.
He who sees all this as fire and Soma, and is not touched by wondrous states, is indeed freed.
One to whom couch, bed and ground are alike, and rice and poor food are alike, is indeed freed.
One to whom linen, kusha bark, silk, bark garments, wool and hide are alike is indeed freed.
He who sees the world as born of five elements and acts accordingly in this world is indeed freed.
One to whom pleasure and pain, gain and loss, victory and defeat, wish and aversion, fear and agitation are equal in every way is indeed freed.
Seeing the body full of blood, urine, excrement and the accumulation of faults, rich in faults, one is freed.
He who sees wrinkles and grey hair, thinness, discoloration and stoop from age is freed.
He who sees in time the loss of manhood, the ceasing of sight, deafness and a mind of breaths is freed.
He who sees sages and gods gone, and asuras who have come, from this world to the next is freed.
Knowing that thousands of lords of the earth, endowed with their various powers, have gone leaving the earth, one is freed.
He who sees wealth hard to get in the world and afflictions easy to get, and the sorrow of family needs, is freed.
Seeing the failings of children and of people, who in the world would not honour liberation?
The man who is awake from scripture and the world, who sees everything, human life as if without essence, is indeed freed in every way.
Hearing this word of mine, you should live as one freed, if your mind is set unwaveringly on liberation while a householder.'
Hearing his words, that lord of the earth, joined with virtues born of liberation, ruled his subjects."
[Yudhishthira said:] "How was the divine sage Ushanas Kavya, of great mind, ever kind to the asuras and unkind to the gods?
Why did he increase the energy of those of immeasurable power? And the Danavas ever bound in enmity with the best of the gods?
And how did Ushanas, of immortal splendour, gain the state of Shukra, and how did he gain prosperity? Tell me all this.
And that radiant one does not go in the middle of the sky; I wish to know this fully, grandsire."
[Bhishma said:] "Hear, king, attentively, all this as it is, as I have heard it before, according to my understanding, sinless one.
This heir of Bhrigu, the sage, true to his firm vows, is kind to the asuras for a compassionate reason.
Indra, and Kubera the king, lord of yakshas and rakshasas, was a powerful lord of the treasury and of the world.
Entering his very self, the great sage perfected in yoga, restraining the god, lord of wealth, by yoga, took away the wealth.
Then Kubera reported it to Shiva of immeasurable splendour, Rudra, best of gods, gentle, of many forms.
[Kubera said:] "Ushanas, of the nature of yoga, restrained me and took my wealth, and having made himself a goal by yoga, went out, the great ascetic."
[Bhishma said:] Hearing this, the great yogi Maheshvara was then angry; his eyes red, king, he stood taking his trident.
Where is he, where is he? he said, taking up the supreme weapon; and Ushanas, knowing his intent, shone from afar.
Knowing that anger of the great yogi, the lord knew his course, his coming and his place.
Thinking of the great-souled Maheshvara with fierce austerity, Ushanas, his self perfected by yoga, appeared at the point of the trident.
His form known, then, by the archer perfected in austerity, and knowing the trident, the lord of the gods bent it with his hand.
With the trident bent by the hand of immeasurable splendour, the lord of fierce weapons called the trident the Pinaka.
Seeing Bhargava in the middle of his hand, Uma's lord, the humped one, opened his mouth and slowly threw him in.
Entering the belly of Maheshvara, the lord, that great soul, the delight of Bhrigu, moved about there.
[Yudhishthira said:] "Why did Ushanas move about in the belly of that wise god of gods, king? And what did that greatly radiant one do?"
[Bhishma said:] "Long ago, gone into the water, of great vows, he stood like a post for ten thousand times a million years, king.
After performing hard austerity he rose from the great lake; then Brahma approached the god of gods.
He asked about the growth of his austerity and his welfare, imperishable; and the bull-bannered one said, "Austerity has been well practised."
Shankara, of great mind, of inconceivable self, ever devoted to truth and dharma, also saw its growth from that union.
With that austerity and wealth, the great yogi shone, great king, mighty in the three worlds.
Then the Pinaka-bearer, of the nature of yoga, entered meditation-yoga; but Ushanas, alarmed, hid in the belly.
And the great yogi praised the god while staying there, and wishing to come out was blocked by his radiance.
Ushanas then said from within the belly, the great sage, "Show me grace," again and again, scourge of foes.
Mahadeva said to him, "Go; liberation is by the organ," having stopped all the openings, bull of the thirty gods.
Not seeing a door, closed on every side, the sage ran about, burning here and there with the radiance.
Coming out by the organ, he attained the state of Shukra; for that reason he does not come in the middle of the sky.
Seeing him come out, blazing as it were with splendour, Bhava, filled with anger, stood with his trident raised.
The goddess restrained the angry lord Pashupati, her husband; and when Shankara was restrained by the goddess, he became her son.
[The goddess said:] "He is not to be killed by you; he has become my son; for no one who has come out of a god's belly meets destruction."
[Bhishma said:] Then he was pleased with the goddess and, smiling, said, "Let him go as he wishes," king, again and again.
Then, bowing to the boon-giving god and the goddess Uma, the wise great sage Ushanas reached the goal he wished.
This has been told to you, dear, the deed of the great-souled Bhargava, best of the Bharatas, that you ask me."
[Yudhishthira said:] "What auspicious deed, best of men, does a man do to gain the highest good here and hereafter? Tell me."
[Bhishma said:] "Here I shall relate to you as before, greatly famous one: King Janaka asked the great-souled Parashara.
'What is the good of all beings, in this world and the next, that should be undertaken? Please tell me.'
Then the sage, joined with austerity, knowing the rules of all dharmas, kindly disposed to the king, spoke.
'Dharma alone done is best here and hereafter; therefore there is nothing higher, as the wise say.
Having taken up dharma, a man is honoured in heaven; the rule of action for embodied beings is of the nature of dharma, best of kings; in it the good in the stages perform their own deeds here.
The course of the world is ordained fourfold, dear; where mortals stay, it proceeds from desire.
Practising good and bad action by various orders, there are many courses for beings divided into ten halves.
The word was made resting on the course of the world and on the Veda, for the peace of the mind, dear; this is not the teaching of the aged.
By eye, mind, speech and action, a fourfold action; as one does action, so he gains.
Action bears fruit unbroken and mixed, king; whether good or bad, it has no destruction.
Sometimes a good deed, dear, stays as if unmoving for one sinking in the world until he is freed from sorrow.
Then, having ended sorrow, he enjoys good deeds; and from the exhaustion of good deeds, bad deeds; know that, lord of men.
Self-control, forbearance, steadiness, energy, contentment, truthfulness, modesty, non-violence, non-addiction and skill: these bring happiness.
A creature should not be unrestrained in bad or good deeds; the discerning should ever strive for collectedness of mind.
He does not enjoy another's good or bad deed; as is the action one does, so he gains.
Having set pleasure and pain in order, a man goes by another; by another goes every person who is joined, king.
What a man would envy in others he should not do himself; the envious joined to it brings ridicule on himself.

The timid kshatriya, the brahmana who eats anything, the vaishya without effort, the low-class idle man, the learned man of no character, the well-born of failed conduct, the brahmana fallen from truth and the bad woman:
the attached freed, the one cooking for himself, the fool who speaks, a king, a poor kingdom: all these, king, come to be pitied, and he who is unjoined and without love for the subjects.'"
[Parashara said:] "With a mind resorting to service, for one without livelihood it is praised; what comes from the hands of the twice-born, not from an equal to one another.
Having gained a life hard to obtain, lord of the people, he should not draw himself down; a man strives for elevation by holy action.
One who has fallen even from his class deserves honour; not the one who, having gained respect, practises rajasic action.
A man gains elevation of class by holy action; not gaining that hard thing, he would destroy it by sinful action.
Sin done through ignorance should be removed by austerity alone; sin bears fruit; sin is self-made; therefore he should not do sin, action whose fruit is sorrow.
An action joined with sin, though it be of great fruit, the wise should not do, like clean water in a bad pool.
What fruit of sinful action do I see? For a good man fallen into misfortune the self does not shine so far.
Even he who, fool, does not undergo remorse here suffers very great torment as he goes.
One who, having himself done sin, then practises the good alone, would be able to do atonement and enjoys both separately.
Violence done unknowingly is removed by non-violence: so the speakers of Brahman say by the direction of the shastra.
And what is done by desire is removed by non-violence too: so say the brahmanas learned in dharmashastra, masters of the Veda.
But I see the action that has been done, endowed with virtue, plain and not joined with sin.
As subtle actions bear fruit here as they are, done with the mind joined to intellect.
An action practised constantly yields little fruit but is strong; one done without forethought, knower of dharma, is done by fierce action.
The actions done by gods and by sages the righteous-souled should not follow, nor, hearing them, blame.
Reflecting in mind, king, knowing his own power, he who does good action sees good things.
As water placed in a new vessel is not lost, so in another than new it is lost; one gains the state well cultivated for happiness."
Then the blessed Agni, the carrier of oblations, showed them his own form, shining, with splendour like the autumn sun.
For in the three worlds, Brihaspati, among the gods I alone have gained Indra-hood, while Marutta is a lord of the earth.
My mind grows weary, and my mouth dries, from advanced age and from the strain of speaking.
Then, seeing Babhru slain, Krishna said to his elder brother, "Wait here for me, Rama, while I put the women in the keeping of their kin."
Without them I cannot dwell here, slayer of Daityas; I wish to go where my brothers have gone.
Your worlds are above the kings' worlds, Yudhishthira, equal to Harishchandra's, Partha, in which you will take your pleasure.
